rule: Table viva station of the day (v6.03). One per day in rotation. Every point must match the named source; add a source for any new station. Never remove stations.

items.q: Which ventilation mode is the Mapleson A efficient for, and what happens when you ventilate through it?
pts: Efficient for spontaneous breathing: the expiratory (APL) valve sits close to the patient, so dead space gas is vented first.
Wasteful for controlled ventilation: fresh gas flow of about 2.5 times minute volume is needed to vent enough alveolar gas and limit rebreathing.
items.pearl: A for spontaneous, D for controlled: the classic order of efficiency is reversed between the two modes.
items.srcT: WFSA Update in Anaesthesia: Anaesthetic breathing systems

items.q: Describe the Bain circuit and its fresh gas needs.
pts: Coaxial Mapleson D: fresh gas runs in the inner tube to the patient end; expired gas travels in the outer tube to the valve and bag.
Spontaneous breathing needs a fresh gas flow of about 2 to 3 times minute ventilation to prevent rebreathing.
Among Mapleson A–D, D is rated the most suitable for controlled ventilation.
items.pearl: Check the inner tube before use: a disconnected or kinked inner tube turns the whole circuit into dead space.
items.srcT: Rose, Byrick, Froese. CO2 elimination with a modified Mapleson D system. Can Anaesth Soc J

items.q: How do you choose an LMA Classic size, and how much should the cuff be inflated?
pts: By weight: 1 up to 5 kg, 1.5 for 5–10, 2 for 10–20, 2.5 for 20–30, 3 for 30–50, 4 for 50–70, 5 for 70–100, 6 over 100 kg.
Inflate to a maximum intracuff pressure of 60 cm H2O; the printed volumes are maximums, not targets.
items.pearl: Measure cuff pressure: over-inflation raises the risk of sore throat and nerve injury without improving the seal.

items.q: How does a pulse oximeter work, and what makes it read wrongly?
pts: Two wavelengths: red 660 nm (deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs more) and infrared 940 nm (oxyhaemoglobin absorbs more).
It looks only at the pulsatile part of the signal, so it measures arterial blood.
Errors: intravenous dyes, low perfusion (low cardiac output, vasoconstriction, hypothermia), dark skin pigmentation, sickle cell disease and ambient light.
items.pearl: 800 nm is the isobestic point, where both haemoglobins absorb equally.
items.srcT: Jubran A. Pulse oximetry. Crit Care 2015

items.q: Compare cutting and pencil-point spinal needles.
pts: Cutting (Quincke) bevel versus pencil-point (Whitacre, Sprotte) with a side hole.
Pencil-point needles cause less post-dural puncture headache, less severe headache and fewer blood patches (meta-analysis of randomised trials).
Smaller gauge also lowers the risk.
items.pearl: Needle gauge and tip design are the two things you control to reduce PDPH.
items.srcT: Cutting vs pencil-point spinal needles and PDPH: a meta-analysis. Medicine 2017

items.q: What dantrolene dose do you give, and how much should be stocked?
pts: Initial dose 2.5 mg/kg, repeated as needed, with a suggested upper limit of 10 mg/kg.
Enough for a 70 kg adult at the upper limit means at least 700 mg: MHAUS suggests a minimum of 36 vials of the 20 mg preparation.
items.pearl: If you are past 10 mg/kg without a response, rethink the diagnosis.
items.srcT: MHAUS: how much dantrolene should be kept on hand

items.q: Give the lipid emulsion regimen for severe local anaesthetic toxicity.
pts: 20% lipid emulsion: bolus 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute, then infusion at 15 mL/kg/h.
Up to two more boluses, 5 minutes apart, if the circulation is not restored or worsens; the rate can be doubled to 30 mL/kg/h.
Do not exceed a cumulative 12 mL/kg.
items.pearl: Propofol is not a substitute for lipid emulsion, and lidocaine is not an anti-arrhythmic here.
items.srcT: AAGBI Safety Guideline: Management of severe local anaesthetic toxicity

items.q: What are the weight-based doses on the paediatric emergency chart?
pts: Adrenaline 10 mcg/kg (1:10,000).
Fluid bolus 10 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid or 0.9% saline.
Glucose 10% 2 mL/kg; sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg; defibrillation 4 J/kg.
items.pearl: Amiodarone 5 mg/kg after the third shock and once more after the fifth.
items.srcT: Resuscitation Council UK / AAP Paediatric emergency drug chart

items.q: Compare the two relaxants for rapid sequence induction.
pts: Suxamethonium: depolarising, satisfactory intubating conditions in about 60 s, cannot be reversed by drugs.
Rocuronium 0.6–1.2 mg/kg: onset is dose dependent; larger doses give block in 60–75 s.
Neostigmine only works at light block; sugammadex reverses rocuronium at any depth, up to 16 mg/kg after a failed intubation.
items.pearl: Know where the sugammadex is before you choose rocuronium for RSI.
items.srcT: Fawcett WJ. Suxamethonium or rocuronium for RSI? BJA Educ 2019

pts: 2 mg/kg when the second twitch of the train-of-four has returned.
4 mg/kg at deep block, with 1–2 post-tetanic counts and no TOF response.
16 mg/kg for immediate reversal about 3 minutes after rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (rocuronium only).
items.pearl: Immediate reversal has not been studied in children.

items.q: Dose, advantages and problems of etomidate.
pts: Induction dose 0.3 mg/kg gives sleep for 4 to 5 minutes; elderly 0.15–0.2 mg/kg.
Only a slight, transient fall in blood pressure.
Single doses can cause transient adrenal suppression; myoclonus and pain on injection are common; contains propylene glycol.
items.pearl: Do not exceed 3 ampoules (30 mL) per procedure.

items.q: Doses of propofol for induction and maintenance.
pts: Adults under 55: 1.5–2.5 mg/kg, titrated (about 40 mg every 10 seconds); less over 55 and in ASA 3–4.
Children over 8 years about 2.5 mg/kg; 1 month to 3 years may need 2.5–4 mg/kg.
Maintenance infusion usually 4–12 mg/kg/h.
items.pearl: Not for induction below 1 month of age.
